en: The Sūtra on the Merit of Making Images Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Ti-yun Prajñā of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven at the Pārijātaka tree.
Beneath a tree, he was together with an immeasurable assembly of great bhikṣus and an immeasurable assembly of great bodhisattvas, with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya as their leader.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in that heavenly realm, observing the three-month rains retreat and preaching the Dharma for his mother; he brought great benefit to the multitude of devas, causing immeasurable devas to leave suffering behind and attain liberation.
Immeasurable devas all received the benefit of the Dharma and attained the fruit of great merit.

At that time, there was a certain son of heaven within that assembly whose lifespan was about to end and who manifested the five signs of decay; by the power of hearing the Dharma, after his life came to an end, he was reborn in this very heaven and forever departed from the evil realms.

At that time, there was no Tathāgata in Jambudvīpa; it was like a dark night when the stars are without the moon, like a country without a sovereign, or like a household without a master. All joy, amusement, and play came to a complete halt.

At that time, sentient beings were solitary and without refuge; they all cherished the Tathāgata with longing in their hearts and gave rise to great sorrow and distress, as if they had lost their parents or as if an arrow had pierced their hearts. Together they went to the places where the World-Honored One had formerly dwelt; seeing the gardens and courtyards entirely empty and devoid of the Buddha, their grief and attachment redoubled, and they could not restrain themselves.

At that time, King Udayana, while residing within his palace, was constantly filled with sorrow and longing for the Buddha. Neither his queens nor his court ladies, nor any source of pleasure, could engage his mind; he thought to himself:
"I am now overwhelmed by grief and sorrow; I shall not live much longer."
"How might I be able to see the Buddha before my life comes to an end?
He then reflected further:
"It is like a person who has someone they love but cannot meet; upon seeing that person's dwelling place or someone resembling them, their grief and distress may be relieved."
He further reflected:
"If I were now to go to the place where the Buddha previously resided and not find him there, my lamentation and grief would be so piercing that I might even bring about my own death."
I observe that there is not a single person in the world who can equal the Tathāgata in physical form, merit, and wisdom.
How may I come to see such a person so as to eliminate my grief and affliction?
Having had this thought, he further reflected:
"I should now fashion an image of the Buddha to pay homage to and make offerings to.
Then, this thought arose again:
"If I create an image that does not resemble the Buddha, I fear I shall incur immeasurable sin.
He further thought:

"Even if all the wise people in the world were to join together in praising the merits of the Tathāgata, they could not exhaust them; yet if a single person praises him according to their own capacity, they will obtain immeasurable merit."
"I am likewise now; I shall create it according to my capacity.
He immediately issued a command to all the artisans within the kingdom, ordering them to assemble.
Once they had gathered, he spoke to them, saying:
"Who can create a physical image of the Buddha for me? I shall reward them handsomely with precious jewels.
The various artisans together addressed the king, saying:
"What Your Majesty now commands is an exceedingly difficult task!"
"The marks and signs of the Tathāgata are peerless in the world.
How could I now possibly create an image of the Buddha?
Even if Viśvakarman, the celestial artisan, were to attempt it, he still could not produce anything resembling the Tathāgata."

If I were to receive the command to fashion an image of the Buddha, I could at most imitate a small portion of the marks such as the usnīṣa and the ūrṇā-kośa; but who else could create all the other marks and signs, the radiance, and the majestic virtue?
"The World-Honored One will surely descend from the heavens; if there should be any deficiency or error in the image we create, our reputations will all be lost!
Having deliberated together in secret, none among us dares to undertake the task."
At that time, the king spoke to him again, saying:
"My mind is resolved; do not decline!
Is it because one cannot drink a river dry that a person suffering from thirst would refuse to drink its water?"
At that time, when the people heard these words of the king, they all came forward, prostrated themselves, and addressed the king together, saying:
"We shall comply with your command!
However, we pray that Your Majesty will grant us leave to deliberate this matter tonight, so that we may proceed with it tomorrow morning."
He further addressed the king, saying:

"For the image Your Majesty now intends to create, you should employ pure purple sandalwood that is dense and firm in its grain and substance. However, as for its form—whether it be seated or standing—and its height and proportions, what should they be?"
The king asked his assembly of ministers about these words, and a wise minister came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"Great King! You should have an image of the Tathāgata seated."

Why is this? Because all Buddhas, having attained great enlightenment, turned the wheel of the true Dharma, manifested great supernormal powers, subdued non-Buddhists, and performed the great works of a Buddha, did so while seated.
"Therefore, one should fashion images of the Teacher seated upon a lion throne in the *baddhaparyaṅka* posture.
At that time, Viśvakarman, the deva, saw this matter from afar and, clearly discerning that the king’s intention was to create an image of the Buddha, reflected thus during the night:
"The skill I possess is the most exquisite; there is no one in the world like me."
"If I were to create it, it should bear at least some resemblance to the Buddha.
He then transformed his body into that of a craftsman, took up various tools, and by the clear dawn, stood beside the king’s gate, instructing the gatekeeper to inform the king in full:
"I now wish to fashion an image for Your Majesty!"
"My craftsmanship is peerless in this world;
I only pray that Your Majesty will not allow others [to do this].
When the King heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy, and he commanded him to enter.
Observing his deportment, he recognized him as a master craftsman and thought to himself:
"How could such a person exist in this world?
Could it not be Viśvakarman, the celestial architect, or perhaps one of his disciples who has come here?"

At that time, the king immediately removed the necklace he was wearing from his own body, held it in his hands, and hung it around her neck; he further promised her various and immeasurable precious treasures.

Then the king, together with his minister in charge of the treasury, selected fragrant wood from the inner storehouse; he carried it upon his own shoulders and presented it to the celestial artisan, saying to him:
"Excellent, O benevolent one!
"You should use this wood to fashion an image for me, so that its form and features resemble those of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the celestial artisan addressed the king, saying:
"Although my craftsmanship is said to be the foremost, I am ultimately unable to fully exhaust the likeness of the Buddha's physical form."
For example, it is as impossible as for someone to draw a sun with charcoal and claim that it resembles the actual sun;
even if one were to fashion a Buddha image out of pure gold, the same would apply.
A non-Buddhist practitioner said, "The Brahma King can create all things in the world, yet he cannot fashion a Buddha image endowed with all the primary and secondary marks!
However, my craftsmanship is supreme among those in the world; therefore, I shall now fashion it for the King!"

This very morning is the eighth day of the month; at this time, when the constellation Puṣya is in conjunction with the appearance of Vibhāvatī, there is this auspicious response marking the Buddha’s initial birth.
"This day is auspicious and celebratory; it is fitting that we begin our work.
Having spoken these words, he took up his axe and began felling the wood; the sound reached upward through the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and arrived at the place where the Buddha was gathered.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, wherever his voice reached, all sentient beings who heard it had their karmic defilements and afflictions completely eliminated.
At that time, the Tathāgata smiled and praised the king’s meritorious virtues in various ways, even bestowing upon him the distant prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Are there currently any among those in the human world who have ever, in a previous life, fashioned an image of the Buddha?"
The Buddha said, "Lord of Devas!
All those who have ever fashioned images of the Buddha were already liberated in the past; they do not even exist among the hosts of devas, much less in any other place."
Only the son of Vaiśravaṇa from the north, Naliśapa, had once in the past fashioned an image of a Bodhisattva; by virtue of this merit, he later became a king named Bimbisāra.
Furthermore, because they saw me, they have now attained birth in the heavens, possessing great power and being forever freed from the evil realms.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and Nadī-Kāśyapa all repaired ancient Buddha halls in past lives; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they have attained eternal liberation.

Gavāmpati was once a cow, seeking water and grass; as he circumambulated the vihāra clockwise, eating various grasses and bamboo, he beheld my honored countenance and gave rise to a heart of joy. By means of this merit, he has now attained liberation.
Śibi once held a precious parasol as an offering to a Buddha image;
Anuruddha likewise offered a single lamp;
and Śūbhana once swept the Buddha hall.
Āmrapālī offered lamps before the Buddha’s image to provide illumination;
the bhikṣu Nanda, out of deep reverence for the Honored One’s majestic form, bathed it with scented water.

There were countless such arhats who all once offered even slight acts of worship at the site of a Buddha image—even down to the most lowly, such as Nagapāla, who, before the seat of an image, made an offering by painting the body of a single image with a small amount of yellow cinnabar. By virtue of this merit, they have all forever left suffering behind and attained liberation.
"Lord of Devas!
If there should be anyone who is able to fashion an image of the Buddha during the time before my Dharma has completely vanished, they shall all attain liberation at Maitreya’s first assembly."

If there are sentient beings who do not seek liberation merely for themselves, but rather create images of the Buddha out of a desire to attain unsurpassed bodhi, you should know that this constitutes the cause for the thirty-two marks, enabling such persons to swiftly achieve buddhahood.
At that time, King Udayana thought to himself,
"How can I ensure that the image I am having made is quickly completed?
Having had this thought, he spoke to the artisan:
"You should apply yourself with diligence so that the work may be swiftly completed, so that I may soon behold it and pay my respects.
At that time, the celestial artisan applied his skillful artistry, concentrating with tireless devotion, and finished it in no time.
The image was seated in the full lotus posture, seven feet in height, with its face, hands, and feet all of a purple-gold color.

When King Udayana saw that the image had been completed, its marks and signs were dignified and majestic; his heart gave rise to pure faith, and he attained the patience of compliance (anulomikī-kṣānti).

Having attained this patience, they were filled with even greater joy and celebration; all their karmic obstructions and various anxieties were completely eliminated, just as mist and dew vanish entirely when the sun rises.
With the sole exception of one karma to be experienced in the present life— due to having previously uttered harsh words toward a noble being—
the king then rewarded that celestial craftsman with various kinds of rare and extraordinary treasures.
At that time, the celestial artisan respectfully addressed the King, saying:
"I rejoice in the King's current creation of this image.
I pray that I may cultivate this merit together with Your Majesty!"
"What Your Majesty has now bestowed, I do not dare accept.
If you insist on giving it to me, please wait for another auspicious day.
Having spoken these words, he immediately ascended back to his own celestial realm that very night.
At that time, the various great kings, including Ajātaśatru and others, had all previously harbored a deep longing for the Buddha in their hearts.
Hearing that the King had completed the construction of the image, they were all filled with joy and celebration.

Together they went to the king’s presence, each making offerings of immeasurable flowers, incense, and music to the Buddha image, and further presenting various rare treasures to the king, all saying these words: “Great King!
"What you have done is truly rare; you have been able to extract from us the poisonous arrows of sorrow and anxiety!

At that time, the Tathāgata was in that celestial realm preaching the Dharma for his mother, and the entire assembly of devas all obtained benefit and joy. Having completed all that was to be done, he again addressed the multitude, saying:
"O sons of the gods!..."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a body of eternal abiding; if there are sentient beings who may be delivered, they immediately manifest to teach and preach the Dharma for them.

When their task is completed and there are no further beings capable of receiving the transformative influence of the Dharma, the Tathāgata ceases to appear therein. Those of limited wisdom claim that the Buddha has truly passed into extinction.
The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, the eternal body; in truth, it does not pass into extinction.
O sons of the gods!
The nature of all Buddhas is thus: they manifest or do not manifest according to the needs of those to be transformed.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again, saying:
"You should know! Those among this assembly of devas who were to be delivered have all been delivered. I now intend to descend to Jambudvīpa."
If you gods should think of me, you ought to apply yourselves with diligent vigor and not be negligent again. Why is this?
Because the fault of negligence prevents you from attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

However, because you have planted roots of merit in the past, you now enjoy these celestial pleasures; yet, becoming attached to negligence and failing to cultivate meritorious deeds, these pleasures will be overtaken by impermanence, and once you fall from them, you will sink for a long time into the evil realms.
Furthermore, you gods have particularly heavy afflictions; upon seeing those superior to yourselves, you immediately give rise to jealousy, never even considering:
"That celestial excellence and pleasure were brought about by the maturation of many meritorious deeds; if I were to practice diligently, I too would surely attain them."

"Furthermore, at present your bodies possess a radiant luster like the first glow of the sun; yet if you harbor jealousy, your minds will become as dark as dead charcoal, and you shall again fall into great darkness where you cannot even see the palm of your own hand, and in the end, you shall become ghosts who feed on vomit."

Furthermore, you gods, who enjoy manifold rewards of merit, whose physical forms are majestic and pure, and whose power and majesty are fierce and courageous—because of jealousy, you shall receive female bodies and forever lose the fierce and courageous strength of a man.
“O sons of the gods!
I recall that in the past there were immeasurable kings, all of whom were unjustly harmed by the jealousy of you [gods].
O sons of the gods!”

In the past, there was an asura king named Ura who practiced austerities and maintained pure moral discipline; yet you gods sent a celestial maiden named Upasī to seduce that king’s heart and cause him to violate his pure conduct.
That king, being stained by attachment, saw his majestic power diminish and was slain by the god Nārāyaṇa; simultaneously, the immeasurable host of asuras was utterly destroyed.
After Nārāyaṇa had slain this king and executed his host, he took the daughter Upasī and departed for the celestial palace.
There was another king named Nahusa; you gods should deceive him with your words and assist the celestial hosts in waging war against the asuras.
Once the asuras have been defeated, you gods turn against them and inflict further harm.

Moreover, because of the lady Śacī, you gods gave rise to anger and jealousy; you concocted slanderous accusations that caused the rishi Agastya to be unjustly suspected, leading him to form an evil vow.
Furthermore, you gods were once deceived and deluded; you said to King Eḍa, "In the abode of the seer there is much pure gold.
The king believed these words and coerced him into producing it.
Because of this, the rishi gave rise to a mind of fierce resentment and immediately killed the king with a blazing fire.

Furthermore, in the past there was a king named Deva who once established a great assembly for the purpose of making offerings; by the sovereign power of the merit from these deeds, he ascended to this heavenly realm and experienced celestial bliss.

"You gods, harboring jealousy in your hearts, have caused [him] to fall from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Jambudvīpa; all his majestic power has been utterly lost, like a moon without light, like a river without water."
"O sons of the gods!

There may be people in the world who possess sovereign majesty and virtue, or who have attained various meditative concentrations, or who have acquired supernormal powers, or who have perfected the four bases of psychic power; yet if they give rise to even a single thought of envy, such merits will all at once be lost."
“Because Devadatta’s ignorance was so profound and heavy, he conceived a spirit of jealousy toward me, and immediately lost his five supernormal powers.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now have a doubt and wish to ask a question.
What is meant by 'jealousy'? He spoke again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who, seeing others superior to themselves, give rise to this thought:
‘How may I obtain what that person has obtained?’”
“Is such a mind as this one of envy? The Buddha said, “No!”
"This is a mind of greed, not envy. Lord of Devas! As for envy:
one seeks fame and profit for oneself and does not desire others to have them; one gives rise to hatred and resentment toward those who possess such things—this is envy."
At that time, the assembly of devas all rose from their seats, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“As the Buddha has instructed, we, the assembly of devas, shall all reverently practice accordingly.”
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is our father, our lord, our honored one, and our supreme one; he has come here out of great compassion for us, bringing benefit to all the hosts of devas.
"Our aspirations are as yet unfulfilled, and we wish to request one further matter of the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
People of the world often treat us gods with great contempt."
Why is this? Because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are born among human beings, and because they attain perfect enlightenment among human beings;
and because among human beings there are many Arhats who have realized the fruits [of the path].

Because Pratyekabuddhas of great majesty and virtue have also appeared among human beings, if the Tathāgata does not now remain here but descends to Jambudvīpa, the people of the world will say that we gods do not know that the Tathāgata possesses great majesty and virtue and should receive the offerings of the gods according to the Dharma; furthermore, they will say that we are unable to make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will remain here for a short while and accept our humble offering, so that those among humans may know that we gods have made offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his silent consent.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You should first go to Jambudvīpa to inquire after the fourfold assembly, saying these words:
'All sentient beings who remember me should assemble in the kingdom of Saṃkāśya.'"
"Seven days from now, you shall all see me.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Having paid homage to the Buddha’s feet, he reached Jambudvīpa in the space of a single blink of an eye and informed the fourfold assembly of the Buddha’s instructions.

At that time, King Udayana and all sentient beings, hearing these words of the Buddha, were filled with such joy and exultation in both body and mind that they were entirely freed from sorrow and affliction, universally attaining a state of refreshing coolness.

At that time, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—wished to travel together to the kingdom of Saṃkāśya. They had already gathered in advance in the city of Rājagṛha and said to one another:

"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is descending to Jambudvīpa; who among us can be the first to receive his respectful salutations and become the leader for all time until the Dharma comes to an end?"
At that time, having heard these words, Mahākātyāyana felt displeased in his heart, fearing that the bhikṣuṇī would become the leader. Why was this?

Within that assembly were two bhikṣuṇīs, Upānanda and Utpalavarṇā, who were highly proficient in penetrating the Dharma-treasury of all Buddhas; their attained supernormal powers were such that none could equal them except for Maudgalyāyana.
Having formed this thought, she rebuked the community of bhikṣuṇīs in various ways.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā addressed the nuns, saying:
"We women, even while living among the laity, are constantly held in high esteem; even those of lowly birth still receive the respect, reverence, service, and offerings of men."

Furthermore, among the bhikṣuṇīs in the Buddha-dharma, many have parents and kinsmen of royal lineage; they are diligent in observing the precepts, do not violate the rules of decorum, and are endowed with all virtuous qualities, yet they are still required to pay homage to even a novice bhikṣu who has recently received the precepts.
Furthermore, Venerable Kātyāyana, you have now again uttered these various reproaches.
I shall provide you with various skillful means to cause the bhikṣuṇīs to surpass them.
Having spoken these words, he immediately set out for the city of Śrāvastī together with the fourfold assembly.

At that time, King Prasenajit, King Ajātaśatru, and King Mahādeva of Vaiśālī each led a fourfold army as their vanguard and retinue; they possessed great power, and the elephants and horses they rode were adorned with various precious objects. With banners, canopies, incense, flowers, and the music of many performers, their majestic appearance was solemn and dignified, resembling that of the devas, as they all likewise proceeded toward the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, King Udayana arrayed his fourfold army as an escort and mounted a great white elephant adorned with rare jewels. Carrying the image he had commissioned upon his own shoulders, he followed it with flowers, banners, and music as offerings, proceeding from his own kingdom toward the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, Viśvakarman and the assembly of devas, knowing that the Buddha was about to descend to Jambudvīpa, constructed three jeweled stairways leading from the city of Saṃkāśya to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The central path of these stairways was made of lapis lazuli; both side paths were made entirely of gold; the places where the feet would tread were laid with white silver; and they were interspersed with the seven treasures of the devas as ornamentation.
At that time, Śakra dispatched messengers to the Yāma Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Nirmāṇarati Heaven, Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahma World, telling them:
"The Tathāgata will soon descend to Jambudvīpa; we wish to make offerings to him, so please come here!"
He again dispatched messengers to the Four Heavenly Kings, the Dragon Kings of the great ocean, the gandharvas, kinnaras, yakṣas, and other assemblies, saying to them:
"The World-Honored One now intends to descend to Jambudvīpa; you should bring whatever you possess here to make offerings!"
When those devas, nāgas, spirits, and others heard these words, there was none who did not gather like clouds in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was atop Mount Sumeru, about to descend with the assembly of devas, all the devas followed him in front and behind; their majestic virtue was blazing and their radiance was magnificent.
Like the full moon in the sky surrounded by the multitude of stars,
or like the rising sun with its radiant hues reflected in the morning clouds—
such was the appearance of the Buddha’s assembly at that time.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, there were five kinds of rare occurrences through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power:
first, it caused those gods not to see the impure things of the human world;
second, it caused all the women to see those celestial males without any thoughts of desire.
Third, it causes men to see the celestial maidens without giving rise to defiled thoughts;
fourth, it enables those in the human realm to behold from afar the various offerings made by the devas;
fifth, although the bodies of the devas are radiant, pure, subtle, and wondrous—beyond the sight of ordinary humans—they can all be clearly perceived through the Buddha’s spiritual power.

At that time, as the World-Honored One descended from the heavens for the first time, his feet stepped upon the jeweled stairway; the Brahma King stood to his right, holding a white parasol in his hand, while Śakra stood to his left, holding a white fly-whisk. The remaining devas all traveled through the void, descending after the Buddha.
At that time, they simultaneously played various kinds of music; each held up banners, streamers, and precious parasols, scattering flowers as an offering.
The hosts of Śuddhāvāsa devas filled the void of space, and hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens held precious jewels and necklaces while singing praises of the Buddha’s virtues.
Furthermore, various devas in the void rained down diverse kinds of incense and diverse kinds of flowers, while the nāgas rained down a fine mist of fragrant rain.
At that time, the sky was pure and free from clouds, and the sound of thunder was exquisite, bringing joy to all who heard it.
The Gandharva gods and Kinnara gods performed subtle melodies of the Devanāga, singing praises of the Tathāgata’s past lives.

At that time, within Jambudvīpa, kings, ministers, commoners, and the fourfold assembly filled the city of Saṃkāśya on all sides; some scattered fragrant flowers, others held banners and canopies, while blowing conchs and beating drums—offering various kinds of music toward the sky—and with hands raised and palms joined, they gazed up in reverence at the Buddha.
Flowers from the realms of humans and devas were scattered from above and below; they fell in profusion and accumulated until they reached his knees.
When the various followers of external paths witnessed this event, they all likewise gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and took refuge, paying him homage with reverence.
At that time, the World-Honored One stepped upon the jeweled stairs and descended step by step until he reached the midpoint of the way.
There, the gods of the Four Great Kings made extensive offerings at that very spot.
"This offering is most sublime; since the beginning of the eon, nothing like it has ever occurred!
At that time, having finished receiving the celestial offerings, the Tathāgata descended the steps together with the great assembly.

When he reached the lowest level and was about to step upon the ground, the bhikṣuṇī Padmāvatī immediately transformed her body into that of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), leading a fourfold army preceded by the seven treasures, descending from the air and arriving swiftly at the Buddha’s location.
The various kings each gave rise to this thought:
"From where has this Wheel-Turning King come?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, seeing the Buddha descend from within his own chamber, immediately adjusted his robes and paid homage from afar.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā relinquished her form as a universal monarch and restored herself to her original appearance; she immediately prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked that bhikṣuṇī in various ways and said to her: "Do you know now?"
Subhūti has already paid homage to me previously.
By whose instruction have you been transformed into a wheel-turning monarch?
That you have been permitted to go forth and receive full ordination exceeds all expectations.
Your wisdom is meager and your deceit is boundless; your compassion and gratitude are like a single drop of dew.
How could you possibly become the foremost among my disciples?
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā felt deep shame and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I now know for myself that my transgressions are not few.”
"From this day forward, we dare not again manifest supernatural powers!
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, the kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly all offered various kinds of ritual implements they held to the Buddha as offerings.
At that time, King Udayana took the Buddha image upon his head, along with various supreme offerings and rare treasures, and went to where the Tathāgata was to present them as an offering.

The Buddha’s body, with its marks and signs of excellence, was perfectly complete and majestic; among all the devas, it was exceptionally distinct and radiant, like the full moon free from the obscuration of clouds.

The images thus created, when compared to the Buddha, are like a mound of earth compared to Mount Sumeru; they cannot serve as a true analogy. Yet, by virtue of possessing the spiral topknot and the white tuft of hair between the brows, they bear a slight resemblance to the Buddha, enabling the fourfold assembly to recognize them as images of the Buddha.
At that time, King Udayana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the past, within the cycle of birth and death, the Tathāgata sought bodhi by practicing immeasurable and boundless difficult and painful austerities, thereby attaining this most supreme and subtle body, which is without equal.”
"The image I have fashioned does not resemble the Buddha; I have reflected upon this in private and consider it a profound fault!
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the king: "It is no fault!"
"You have now already performed immeasurable benefit; there is no one else who can equal you.
You are now the first to establish the standard within my Buddha-dharma; by these causes and conditions, you cause immeasurable sentient beings to attain the great benefit of faith."
"You have now already attained immeasurable merit and vast roots of goodness.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again addressed the king, saying:
"O King, do not harbor anxiety or fear regarding this!"
The Tathāgata, while previously in the heavens and here in this human world, has praised everywhere the merit of the King’s creation of the image; all the hosts of devas likewise rejoice in it.
"In future ages, those who possess faith will all, because of this king, create images of the Buddha and thereby obtain supreme merit.
Your Majesty should now rejoice and congratulate yourself!"
The Sūtra on the Merit of Casting Images Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.
The Sūtra on the Merit of Casting Images Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne at the site of enlightenment in the city of Śrāvastī.
Then, the fourfold assembly each thought in their hearts:
"We wish to hear the Tathāgata expound upon the merits of creating images."
“If there are sentient beings who fashion images of the Buddha, even if they do not resemble him, how much merit will they obtain?

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, knowing their thoughts, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"Now King Udayana is having an image of the Buddha fashioned. Whether the Buddha is still in the world or has already entered parinirvāṇa, for those who possess faith and are able to follow suit in creating such an image, we pray that the World-Honored One will extensively explain the characteristics of the merit they shall obtain!"
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: “Maitreya,
listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!
I shall now speak for you.

If there be sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who single-mindedly focus their minds on the Buddha’s merits, constantly contemplating the Tathāgata’s majestic power and sovereignty—endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great kindness and great compassion, the wisdom of all-knowledge, the thirty-two marks of a great man, and the eighty secondary characteristics; wherein every single pore emits immeasurable rays of light of various colors, adorned and perfected by hundreds of thousands of billions of kinds of supreme merit and virtue; possessing immeasurable wisdom, clearly penetrating and thoroughly understanding immeasurable samādhis, immeasurable dharmas of patience, immeasurable dhāraṇīs, and immeasurable supernormal powers.
All such merits as these are immeasurable, free from all faults, and without equal.

When this person contemplates and reflects upon them with such earnest attention, giving rise to deep faith and joy, and fashions a Buddha image based on the various marks and signs, their merit will be vast, immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation.

“Maitreya! If there is someone who uses various colored threads to create a painted image, or fashions one by casting gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, tin, and so forth; or carves one from sandalwood and other fragrant woods; or constructs one using a combination of pearls, conch shells, brocades, and woven silks; or uses red earth, white lime, clay, or wood—whichever materials they have according to their means—to create a Buddha image, even as small as a single finger’s breadth, such that those who see it recognize it as the Honored One’s countenance, I shall now describe the karmic reward for that person.”

“Maitreya! Although such a person may still wander within the cycle of birth and death, they will never be born into a poor family, nor will they be born in a peripheral or minor land, a low-caste lineage, or a solitary household. Furthermore, they will not be born among the Mlecchas, nor in families of merchants, peddlers, laborers, butchers, or meat-sellers; nor will they be born into base or humble artisan lineages, impure clans, heretical ascetic groups, or families of wrong views—unless by the power of a specific vow, they shall never be born in such places.”
Such a person will always be born into the lineage of a universal monarch (cakravartin) of great power, or into a family of pure-living brahmins who are wealthy, sovereign, and free from faults.
In whatever place they are born, they will always encounter the Buddhas, serving and making offerings to them.
Alternatively, they may become kings who are able to uphold the True Dharma, transforming others through the Dharma and never practicing unrighteous ways.

Or they may become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, perfected with the seven treasures and endowed with a thousand sons; traveling through the air, they transform the four continents, enjoying sovereign abundance and happiness for the duration of their entire lifespan.

Or they may become Śakra, the King of the Yāma Heaven, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; they shall experience all the joys of humans and devas, and such meritorious rewards will continue in succession without end.

In whatever place they are born, they will always be male and never receive a female body; furthermore, they shall not receive the bodies of eunuchs, those with dual sexual organs, or those of lowly status.

The bodies they receive will be free from all ugliness: their eyes will not be blind or squinting; their ears will not be deaf or impaired; their noses will not be crooked or twisted; their mouths will not be slanted or askew; their lips will not hang down, nor will they be wrinkled or parched; their teeth will not be sparse or missing, nor black or yellow; their tongues will not be short or constricted; their necks will have no goiters or tumors; their forms will not be hunched; their complexions will not be mottled; their arms will not be stunted; their feet will not be lame or crippled;
they will not be excessively thin, nor excessively fat, nor too tall, nor too short. Thus, none of these unpleasant characteristics shall exist at all.

His body was upright and well-proportioned; his facial features were perfect and complete. His hair was deep blue-black, soft, lustrous, and pure. His lips were like vermilion fruit; his eyes were like blue lotuses. His tongue was broad and long; his teeth were white, even, and closely set. His speech was skillful and eloquent, capable of bringing joy to all who heard it.

His arms and elbows are long and well-proportioned; his palms are flat, even, and thick; his waist and thighs are full and robust; his chest is broad and expansive; his hands and feet are soft like *tūla* cotton; he is endowed with all the marks of perfection without any deficiency, possessing great physical strength like that of the god Nārāyaṇa.

“Maitreya! It is as if there were a person who had fallen into a privy. Having emerged from it, they scraped away the filth and washed themselves with pure water; they then anointed their body with fragrance and put on fresh, clean clothes.”
In this way, while such a person is still inside the latrine and has not yet emerged, how can the pure and the impure, the fragrant and the foul, be compared?
These matters are vastly separated; there is no equality or proportion between them.

Maitreya! If there is a person who, amidst the cycle of birth and death, is able to give rise to faith and fashion an image of the Buddha, the difference between them and when they had not yet fashioned it is as vast and remote as this.
It should be known that wherever this person is born, they will purify their karmic obstructions; they will spontaneously understand various arts and crafts without a teacher.
Though born in the human realm, they possess the six faculties of a deva;
if born among the devas, they will transcend all other devas.

In whatever place they are born, they shall be free from all ailments and suffering; they shall have no scabies or leprosy, no carbuncles or abscesses, and shall not be possessed by malevolent spirits.

They shall be free from such diseases as insanity and consumption, jaundice and malaria, tumors and malignant sores, chronic ailments, excessive vomiting and diarrhea, indigestion, and general body aches; likewise, the four hundred and four types of diseases, including hemiplegia and lameness, shall all be entirely absent.

Furthermore, they shall not be harmed by such adverse conditions as poisons, weapons, tigers, wolves, lions, water, fire, or hostile bandits; they will always attain fearlessness and shall not commit any transgressions.

“Maitreya! If there are sentient beings who, having committed evil karma in their past lives, are destined to undergo various forms of suffering and affliction— namely, shackles and fetters, beatings and verbal abuse, being burned or roasted, having their skin flayed or hair plucked out, being bound upside down and suspended high,
or even having their limbs and joints severed— if they give rise to a mind of faith and fashion images of the Buddha, they shall not undergo any such retributive suffering.”
They shall not be born in places where bandits and rebels cause incursions and disturbances, where cities and towns are destroyed, or where there are portents of evil stars, famine, or pestilence.
"If one says that there is birth, this is a false statement.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata has always taught that wholesome and unwholesome karmas are never lost or destroyed.
If there are sentient beings who commit various grave offenses, they shall be born into families of low and base lineage, suffering from poverty and illness, with their lifespans cut short.
"If they later give rise to faith and fashion images of the Buddha, will they still have to undergo the retribution for these various sins, or not?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
“Maitreya! Listen attentively now;
I shall explain it for you.”

If those sentient beings, having committed various transgressions, resolve their minds to create images, seek refuge through repentance, and firmly sever themselves from such acts, vowing never to commit them again, all that they previously did shall be completely extinguished.
I shall now explain this matter to you in detail. Maitreya!

It is as if there were a person who, due to past conduct characterized by stinginess, undergoes the suffering of poverty because of those conditions; he possesses no wealth or treasures, and his resources are utterly depleted.

If one should happen to encounter a bhikṣu who has previously entered the meditative absorption of cessation and is just emerging from that concentration, and should immediately offer food and drink with reverence and devotion, this person, having made such an offering, will forever abandon poverty; whatever they require shall be fulfilled exactly according to their wishes.
“Maitreya! Where now are that poor man’s evil karmas from previous lives and the retributions he received?
Maitreya Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
By virtue of giving food, all evil karma from previous lives has been completely extinguished; we are forever freed from poverty and have become abundantly wealthy.
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! It is as you have said.

You should know that this person is likewise; by virtue of having fashioned the image, all those evil karmas will be exhausted without remainder, and the retributions they were destined to undergo shall no longer be experienced.”

Maitreya! There are three kinds of karma: first, that which is experienced in the present life; [second, that which is experienced in the next life; and third, that which is experienced in subsequent lives].
Second, karma to be experienced in the present life;
third, karma to be experienced in future lives.
Within these three types of karma, each has both determinate and indeterminate aspects.
"If a person with faith creates an image of the Buddha, only a small portion of their determinate karma (*niyata-karma*) will be accepted [as maturing], while all the rest will not be accepted.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The Tathāgata has always taught that there are five types of karma that are most grave and heavy, which inevitably lead to rebirth in the Avīci Hell: namely, killing one's father, harming one's mother, killing an Arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha with a malicious and rebellious mind, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
If there are sentient beings who first commit such offenses, but later give rise to pure faith toward the Buddha and fashion images of the Buddha, will these people fall back into hell?
"Will they not fall?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!"
I shall now speak another parable for you.

Suppose there were a person who, holding a powerful bow in his hand, shot an arrow upward at the leaves within a forest; the arrow would pass right through them, meeting with no obstruction whatsoever.

If there are sentient beings who have committed such a heinous crime as parricide, yet later fashion an image of the Buddha and repent with a sincere heart, they will attain rootless faith and their sense of self-identity will become thin and slight; though they fall into hell, they will immediately emerge from it, like an arrow that does not linger—this case is just like that.

Furthermore, it is like a bhikṣu who has attained the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhividhi-jñāna), who goes from this shore of the ocean to the other shore and traverses the four continents without anyone being able to obstruct him.
This person is likewise: although he temporarily falls into hell due to a prior transgression, his past karma is unable to act as an obstruction.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, are the Dharma-nature body; they are not bodies of physical form.”

If one were to regard the physical marks as the Buddha-body, then the bhikṣu Nanda and the Wheel-Turning Sage King would both be Buddhas, for they both fully possess all the primary and secondary marks.

Suppose there are sentient beings who destroy the Buddha’s Dharma-body, declaring the Dharma to be non-Dharma and non-Dharma to be Dharma; yet later, they give rise to faith and create images of the Buddha—will such grave offenses also be extinguished?
"Is it because they cannot attain cessation?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!"

If those sentient beings proclaim what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, or proclaim the Dharma as what is not the Dharma, yet do so merely with their words without corrupting their views, and subsequently develop faith and joy by fashioning images of the Buddha, their prior evil karma will result only in a light retribution within this very life; they shall not fall into the evil realms, yet they will not immediately attain liberation from birth and death.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is someone who steals property from a Buddha-stūpa, or property belonging to the Saṃgha, property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, or property belonging to the present Saṃgha, and uses it for themselves or gives it to others, regarding it as their own property;”
The World-Honored One has often said that those who misappropriate the property of a Buddha stūpa or the property of the Saṃgha commit a most grave offense.

Now, if such sentient beings, having committed these offenses, feel deep remorse and self-reproach, and then give rise to pure faith to create images of the Buddha—will such offenses as these be extinguished?

I shall now speak a parable for you.

Suppose there is a poor man who previously owed many debts; he suddenly encounters a hidden treasure and obtains immeasurable jewels. Having repaid his debts, he possesses a surplus of wealth for the rest of his life.

"You should know that this person is likewise so; by repaying that object with double its value and further creating an image of the Buddha, they shall be freed from all suffering and affliction, and forever attain peace and happiness.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
As the Buddha has taught, one who commits a *pārājika* offense within the Buddha-dharma is not said to be "born" [into it].

Yet, if there is someone who, after committing such a sin, resolves their mind to recollect the merits of the Buddhas and fashions an image of the Buddha, will they attain rebirth within the Buddha-dharma?
"Furthermore, have you attained realization of the Dharma in this life, or in a second, third, or fourth life?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!"
For example, suppose there is a person whose body is bound by five fetters; if they attain liberation, they will be like a bird escaping from a net and reaching a place of unimpeded freedom.

This person is just the same: if they give rise to faith and, recollecting the Buddha’s merits, fashion an image of the Buddha, all karmic obstructions will be completely eliminated, and they will swiftly emerge from the cycle of birth and death without hindrance.
Maitreya, you should know that there are three vehicles: namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle.
Whichever vehicle such a person aspires to and delights in, they shall attain liberation through that very vehicle.

If one seeks only to attain Buddhahood and does not pursue other rewards, then even though one possesses heavy obstacles, they shall be swiftly extinguished; even while remaining within birth and death, one shall be free from suffering and hardship; and until one realizes unsurpassed Bodhi, one shall obtain a pure land, be endowed with all the primary and secondary marks, and the lifespan attained shall be eternally inexhaustible.
At that time, there were those in the assembly who had not yet resolved their minds toward the Mahāyāna, and they all gave rise to doubts:
"Did the Tathāgata, in the past, create images of the Buddha, or did he not?"
If he were a creator, why would his lifespan have limits, why would he be subject to illness and suffering,
and why would the land he inhabits be so defiled and turbid rather than pure?
At that time, King Prasenajit, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I have observed that the Tathāgata’s faculties, marks, and signs, as well as his lineage, are all preeminent; my mind is resolved upon this, and I have no doubt.”
Nevertheless, at one time the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had his foot wounded by a splinter from a *khadira* tree;
on another occasion, he encountered stones hurled from a mountain by Devadatta, which injured his foot and caused it to bleed;
and once again in the past, he declared that he was ill and ordered Jīvaka to prepare a medicine for diarrhea.
Furthermore, on one occasion he suffered from a back ailment, and by having Mahākāśyapa recite the seven factors of enlightenment, his suffering was relieved;
on another occasion, when he had an illness, he sent Ānanda to the house of a brahmin to beg for cow’s milk;
and on yet another occasion, during a three-month retreat in the village of Sālā, he subsisted solely on horse fodder.
Furthermore, on one occasion, he went out to beg for alms but received nothing, returning with his bowl empty.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"If there is anyone who creates an image of the Buddha, all their karmic obstructions shall be eliminated; they shall be free from all suffering and affliction, and shall have no diseases."
"Did the World-Honored One create images in the past, or did he not?
If he created Buddha-images in former times, for what reason do such events as these now occur?"
The Buddha said to King Prasenajit:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well."
I shall now explain this in detail for Your Majesty. Great King!

In past ages, while seeking enlightenment, I fashioned Buddha images using various jewels, sandalwood, and painted colors; such images exceed in number the total count of humans and devas present in this assembly.
By virtue of this merit, although he remains within the cycle of birth and death and has not yet exhausted all afflictions, the body he receives is as firm as a diamond and cannot be destroyed.
Great King!

I recall that in the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas of birth and death, I fashioned images of the Buddha; even then, I was still accompanied by and associated with immeasurable afflictions such as greed and anger.

Yet, never for even a single moment, due to the influence of sinful karma, have I experienced the disharmony of the four great elements, nor the various sufferings of illness caused by malevolent spirits; there was nothing among my necessities that was not fully provided. How much less, now that I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, could there be such undesirable circumstances?
"Great King!

If, having previously fashioned an image of the Buddha, I were now to receive this retribution due to residual karma, how could I then dare to speak fearlessly, saying that the creation of a Buddha image definitely enables one to exhaust all evil karma?"
"Great King!
In the past, I bestowed immeasurable food, drink, wealth, and treasures; why is it that at this present time, when I beg for alms, I do not receive them and must eat horse fodder?"

If this matter were actually true, why would I have praised the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) in various ways throughout immeasurable sūtras, declaring that its meritorious karma is never in vain?
"Great King!
I am one who speaks the truth and one who does not speak deceptively.
If I were to deceive you, how much more so would others?"
"Great King!

I have long since severed all evil karma; I am able to renounce what is difficult to renounce and perform what is difficult to perform. I have sacrificed my body and life more than hundreds of thousands of billions of times, and I have fashioned immeasurable images of the Buddhas. I have already repented for immeasurable sinful karmas—how could I possibly be subject to such things as physical injury, the suffering of illness, eating horse barley, or hunger and thirst?"
If one who has previously attained a superior fruit now regresses and loses it, why would it be necessary to exhort them to cultivate these various merits and virtues?
Great King!
The eternal body and dharma-body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas manifest such events for the sake of delivering sentient beings; they are not actual [regressions].

The injury to his foot, the ailment of his back, the begging for milk, the taking of medicine, up to his entry into nirvana and the distribution of his relics to erect stupas—all these were the Tathāgata’s skillful means, causing all sentient beings to perceive such signs.
"Great King!

When I manifest such various calamities in the world, it is because I wish to show sentient beings that the retribution of karma is never lost, so that they may give rise to fear, sever all transgressions, and cultivate various wholesome deeds. Only then will they come to understand that the eternal body and the dharma-body possess limitless lifespans and that their lands are pure."
"Great King!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are free from falsehood; because they possess great compassion, wisdom, and skillful means, they are able to manifest such various displays."

At that time, having heard these words, King Prasenajit was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; together with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, he all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

There are women whose aspirations are narrow and small, who harbor much jealousy and anger, who are frivolous, fickle, and crooked, who do not relinquish resentment, and who do not repay kindness. Even if they seek bodhi, they are unable to maintain it steadfastly; they constantly desire to deceive all sentient beings, and they themselves are likewise deceived by others.”
World-Honored One!
If this woman were to create an image of the Buddha, would such karmic deeds be extinguished?
Would she be able to become a valiant man in the future and seek the fruit of Buddhahood?
Can you become one who recognizes and repays kindness?
Can you possess wisdom and great compassion?
Are you able to cultivate weary detachment toward the phenomena of birth and death?

"Except for those who, through the power of their vows, have attained a state where they will never again receive a female body—such as Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the Buddha’s mother, Lady Māyā—is this not so?
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Maitreya!"
If there is a woman who can create an image of the Buddha, she shall never again receive a female body.
Even if she should receive such a body, she will become a "Woman-Jewel" (strī-ratna), supreme and foremost among women.
However, there are five kinds of virtues possessed by women, and the virtues attained by this woman surpass those of all other women.
What are these five?
First, she gives birth to children.
Second, noble lineage; third, an upright and virtuous nature;
fourth, extraordinary physical characteristics.
Fifth, her physical appearance is beautiful and upright. “Maitreya!
All women constantly receive a female body due to eight causes and conditions.”
What are the eight?
First, a fondness for the female body;
second, an attachment to female desire.
Third, her mouth constantly praises the beauty and physical qualities of other women;
fourth, her mind is not upright, as she conceals her own actions;
fifth, she feels weary of and holds in contempt her own husband.
Sixth, to hold others in high esteem;
seventh, to recognize the kindness of others while one’s own conduct is contrary and rebellious;
eighth, to use false and deceptive adornments with the desire to cause others to become infatuated.

If one can forever sever these eight matters and fashion images of the Buddha, they shall remain a man until the attainment of Buddhahood; it is impossible for them to ever again receive a female body.
“Maitreya! There are four causes and conditions that cause men to receive the body of a woman. What are these four?
First, to mock and call out to the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and all noble ones with the light, frivolous voice of a woman;
second, to speak with a slanderous mind against those who purely uphold the precepts, claiming they have violated them;
third, to delight in practicing flattery and deception to delude others.
Fourth, upon seeing others who surpass oneself, one gives rise to envy in the heart.
If a man commits these four acts, after his life ends he will inevitably receive a female body and further undergo the sufferings of immeasurable evil realms.

If one develops deep faith, repents of what was previously done, and fashions an image of the Buddha, then all those offenses will be extinguished, and one will certainly never again receive retribution as a woman.
“Maitreya! There are four causes and conditions that cause men to receive the body of a eunuch. What are these four?
First, harming the bodies of others, even down to animals;
second, feeling anger or derision toward śramaṇas who uphold the precepts, and slandering or defaming them;
third, having a mind full of greed and desire, and thus violating the precepts intentionally.
Fourth, those who personally violate the precepts and further encourage others to do so;

yet, if there is a man who first committed such an act but later gives rise to faith and fashions images of the Buddha, he shall not suffer this retribution upon attaining Buddhahood, but will always be born as a man with all his faculties complete.
“Maitreya! There are four kinds of karma that cause a man to receive a body with two sexual organs, making him the lowest among all people.
What are these four?
First, to commit lewd acts against those who are worthy of respect;
second, to have sexual attachment toward improper places on a male body;
third, to engage in sexual acts with oneself.
Fourth, [there are those who] entice women and sell them to others.

If there are sentient beings who have previously committed such an act, they should deeply reproach themselves, repent for their former transgressions, give rise to pure faith, and fashion images of the Buddha; until they attain Buddhahood, they shall no longer receive such a body.
“Maitreya! Furthermore, there are four conditions by which the minds of men constantly give rise to desire for women, and they take pleasure in others performing the acts of a man toward themselves.”
What are the four? First, out of resentment or for sport, slandering and disparaging others;
second, delighting in making women’s clothing and ornaments.
Third, engaging in sexual misconduct with female relatives;
fourth, falsely accepting the veneration of others despite lacking genuine superior virtues.
By these causes and conditions, they cause men to give rise to such distinct afflictions.

If one repents past transgressions and does not create new ones, and with a mind of faith and joy fashions an image of the Buddha, their offenses will be extinguished and this [afflictive] mind will also cease.
“Maitreya! There are five kinds of stinginess that can destroy sentient beings.
What are these five?
First, those who are stingy regarding the neighboring villages where they dwell shall be reborn in the wilderness;
second, those who are stingy regarding the houses and dwellings where they reside shall become possessed by malevolent spirits and constantly dwell amidst filth and excrement;
third, those who are stingy regarding their handsome features and beautiful complexion shall experience the retribution of an ugly and unpleasant form.
Fourth, by being stingy with all one's wealth and possessions, one shall suffer poverty and a lack of food and clothing;
fifth, by being stingy with the Dharma one has learned, one shall receive the retribution of being dull-witted, such as among animals.
If one repents of one's past karma and creates a majestic image of the Buddha, one will forever be free from avarice and shall not suffer the retribution previously mentioned. "Maitreya!
Furthermore, there are five conditions that cause sentient beings to be born in frontier regions or during times when the Buddha-dharma does not exist."
What are these five?
First, failing to give rise to pure faith toward the Three Jewels, the field of merit;
second, turning one's back on reality and violating principle while falsely dispensing instructions.
Third, to provide instruction that is not in accordance with reality;
fourth, to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, resulting in two factions;
fifth, to cause even as few as two bhikṣus to become discordant.
If one permanently severs such karma and creates images of the Buddha, then one will always encounter the appearance of Buddhas and constantly hear the essentials of the Dharma. "Maitreya!

Furthermore, there are five kinds of causes and conditions by which sentient beings are constantly loathed and shunned by others, such that even their closest relatives do not rejoice at the sight of them."
What are the five? First, divisive speech;
second, harsh speech; [and so forth].
Third, they engage in much quarreling;
fourth, they harbor much anger;
fifth, they employ skillful speech that mimics the truth in order to practice slander.

If, later on, they resolve their minds to create images of the Buddha, repent of their previous evil karma, and vow never to commit it again, all the transgressions they have committed will be eradicated, and they will be loved and respected by all people.

Why is this? Because all Buddhas possess immeasurable and boundless superior merit and virtue; immeasurable and boundless great wisdom; and immeasurable and boundless various rare qualities such as samādhis and liberations.

“Good son! Suppose there were someone who ground the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system into fine dust, and then further crushed that dust so that each individual particle was equal in number to the total number of dust particles in those three-thousandfold great thousandfold world systems; suppose there were as many such three-thousandfold great thousandfold world systems as there would be from crushing that dust.”

Suppose there were a person who took a single fragment of dust and, by means of supernormal power, traveled toward the eastern direction, passing as many trichiliocosm world-systems in a single *kṣaṇa* as there are atoms in that fragment of dust. Let the second, third, and all subsequent *kṣaṇas* be likewise; continuing until the end of those kalpas equal in number to the atoms in the fragment of dust, let every *kṣaṇa* within those kalpas each constitute one kalpa. Having passed through that many kalpas, moment by moment, he traverses as many trichiliocosm world-systems in each *kṣaṇa* as there were atoms in the original fragment of dust.

Having finished this, he then drops this particle of dust; the man returns, takes another particle of dust, and again goes toward the east, passing twice as far as before, drops that dust, and returns. This continues until he reaches the third particle of dust, which is twice the distance of the second.
In this manner, they increase successively by multiples of the preceding amount, until reaching the total number of these pulverized atoms.
As it was said for the eastern direction, so it is likewise for the south, west, and north.
If all the lands through which this person has traveled in the four directions were ground into dust,
and if all sentient beings together were to calculate and measure those atoms, they might be able to know their number;
yet the merit contained within a single pore of the Tathāgata’s body cannot be known!
Why is this? Because all the merits of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are immeasurable and inconceivable.
"O son of good family!

Even if the wisdom possessed by all such śrāvakas as Śāriputra were as numerous as the atoms described previously, it would not equal the wisdom of a single thought-moment of the Tathāgata. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata is able, in every moment of thought, to constantly manifest various immeasurable and supreme merits—such as samādhis, liberations, and dhāraṇīs—that exceed the number of atoms in the dust of the ten directions;
as for the merits of the Buddhas, even all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know them even by name.

Therefore, if one possesses a heart of pure faith and creates an image of the Buddha, all karmic obstructions will be eliminated without exception; the merit obtained will be immeasurable and boundless, leading ultimately to the attainment of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and the eternal uprooting of all suffering and affliction for sentient beings.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, King Udayana, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sutra on the Merit of Casting Images Spoken by the Buddha, Volume II.
